control_ladder.note_beginner: Look the trunk and branches over while the tree is bare in winter. White peach scale shows up as snow-white patches on the bark that scrape off easily, and on a small tree, if only a few twigs or branches carry a heavy crust, cut those off and get them away from the tree. That takes the colonies out along with the wood they are fixed to, and nothing you spray afterward has to cover them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Dormant pruning is the natural inspection pass, since white peach scale sits on the trunk and limbs where the bare tree makes it obvious. UC IPM's condition is specific: prune off heavily infested twigs and branches only when they are limited to a few parts of a small plant, which makes this a pruning-out-colonies move rather than a treatment for a tree encrusted end to end. Florida's guide adds a warm-weather cue, since the white patches are most visible when the males emerge.

control_ladder.note_beginner: First see whether ants are climbing the tree. White peach scale gives off no honeydew, so ants have no reason to visit it; a trail of ants on a persimmon means something that makes honeydew is there: one of the soft scales (Georgia expects tuliptree scale), mealybugs, or the persimmon psyllid, any of which drips the sugary honeydew ants collect. Ants defend the insects they tend against the ladybugs and small wasps that eat them, so keep the ants off: put a band of heavy paper or tree wrap around the trunk, spread a sticky barrier on the band and not on the bark itself, and remove any branch or weed that lets ants walk in from the ground or a wall.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Scoped to the soft-scale part of the picture: armored scales such as white peach scale produce no honeydew, so there is nothing for ants to tend and a barrier buys nothing against them. Where the scale is a soft species and ants are working it, UC IPM's instruction is to control the ants because they attack the parasites and predators of scale, and to deny them the canopy by pruning bridging branches or weeds and applying a sticky material to the trunk over a wrap. It restores the biological control the next step relies on rather than acting on the scale itself.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On an unsprayed persimmon, scale is usually held down for you. Georgia's guide says that where nothing is sprayed, scale is generally kept under control by natural parasites, predators and diseases, and that spraying for other pests often lets scale loose from that control. So the main thing is what you do not do: keep strong, broad insect sprays off the tree, and the ladybugs, lacewings and small parasitic wasps that attack scale will keep working.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conservation is the operative control here, and the persimmon documents say so directly: UGA has scale generally kept under control by parasites, predators and diseases in unsprayed situations, with sprays made for other pests the usual reason it escapes; UF names ladybird beetles and lacewings for biological control; UC IPM advises against foliar broad-spectrum insecticides whose residues persist for weeks. A scale flare on a persimmon is worth reading as a question about what was sprayed last season before it is read as a call for a spray this one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When scale is spreading in spite of all that, horticultural oil is the spray both Georgia and Florida point to, and the time for it is late winter, shortly before the buds swell, while the tree is still bare. Oil kills by coating and smothering, so it only works on scale it actually wets: soak the bark of the trunk, the limbs and the ends of the branches. Skip it on a drought-stressed tree and on days above 90°F, when it can scorch the tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Dormant oil is the documented direct control: UGA has an application shortly before bud swell giving good control, and UF's cell is a 3% dormant oil before bud break, with summer oil as the in-season alternative. UC IPM supplies the reasoning behind the timing: overwintering scale on a deciduous tree is reached by thoroughly spraying the bark of terminal shoots in winter, and an in-season oil works only when applied soon after most crawlers have emerged and the scales are still young nymphs, which a band of double-sided sticky tape around an infested twig in spring will show you. Coverage governs the result, and oil stays off a water-stressed tree and out of heat above 90°F.

Where the scale is a soft species, such as the tuliptree scale Georgia expects, the colony also drips sticky honeydew that grows black sooty mold and draws ants; white peach scale and the other armored scales produce no honeydew at all.

If the bumps are one of the soft scales instead, you will also find a sticky coating (honeydew) on the leaves and branches below them that turns black with mold and brings ants. White peach scale makes no honeydew, so a crusty trunk with no stickiness is the usual persimmon picture.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If mealybugs have built up on a persimmon, look for ants on the trunk first. Ants feed on the honeydew mealybugs give off and, in return, keep the beetles and small wasps that eat mealybugs away from them, so a colony with ants tending it grows where one left alone would fade out. Put a band of heavy paper or tree wrap around the trunk, coat the band with a sticky barrier (never the bare bark), and trim any low branch that touches the ground, a fence or another plant so the ants have no way around it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's mealybug guidance is to keep ants out of infested plants because ants protect mealybugs from their natural enemies, and on a persimmon the ant trail up the trunk is the thing to break. Florida's persimmon table makes the same point from the psylla side, where mealybugs turn up in the same curled leaves and the ants feeding on the honeydew may also need controlling. A sticky band over a trunk wrap and the removal of bridging branches restore the predation this pest is normally held by.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where the cottony clumps sit out in the open on shoots or branches, turn the hose on them at full pressure; a persimmon is sturdy enough to take it, and a good many mealybugs are dislodged that way. Choose a morning so the foliage has the day to dry off, and count on going back over the tree, since some always cling on.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM allows that on sturdy plants a high-pressure or forcible water spray can reduce mealybugs that are somewhat exposed; it does nothing for colonies tucked into crotches and crevices, so it is a knock-back on visible clusters, with no residue and no cost to the natural enemies.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Outdoors, most mealybugs are eaten before they matter. Ladybugs, lacewings and small parasitic wasps keep them below damaging levels on garden trees, and persimmon is a crop with few serious insect problems to begin with. Keep strong, broad-spectrum insect sprays off the tree so those helpers stay.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Natural enemies are the standing control: UC IPM's statement is that most species have natural enemies that keep populations below damaging levels in landscapes and gardens, with the mealybug destroyer lady beetle the predator it singles out, and its fruit-tree note is that citrus has the most problems while on stone and pome fruits mealybugs are rarely at damaging levels, a scope that stops short of persimmon. Georgia calls oriental persimmon relatively free of serious insect problems, which is the reading behind this pest's low grade. Preserving the enemies means avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides for any pest in the area, not just this one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For clumps that keep coming back, spray insecticidal soap straight onto them. Soap works only where it lands and only on what it wets, and the waxy coating sheds a lot of it, so the young ones with less wax are the ones it reaches best. Plan on more than one go, and keep it off a dry, stressed tree or a day over 90°F.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM rates soaps, horticultural oils and neem as giving some suppression when applied directly on mealybugs, especially against younger nymphs with less wax accumulation. Suppression is the right word: the wax defeats a single wetting, colonies sit in crevices a spray runs past, and there is no residual. Spot application, repeated and confined to the clumps you can see, is the useful form; a blanket spray costs beneficials for little gain.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Soft, oval insects covered in white wax, gathered in the protected places on a tree: branch crotches, the base of a stem, between a stem and a leaf lying against it, and, on persimmon, inside the leaves curled by persimmon psylla. Their sticky honeydew, the black sooty mold that grows on it, and ants feeding on it are often the first signs. Persimmon carries few serious insect problems, and mealybugs are reported on it as an occasional case.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Most years this one takes care of itself. Georgia's advice is that the psyllid is often held down by natural parasites and that you should not spray until you have actually seen damage; North Carolina's note, written for native persimmon, is that its numbers soon fall on their own as parasitic wasps and other enemies go to work. So leave the curled leaves alone, keep harsh insect sprays off the tree, and let the helpers finish. If the tree is being stunted and you decide to act, the material North Carolina names is horticultural oil, which smothers the psyllids without leaving a residue that hurts the helpful insects, and it has to go on at the first spring flush, because once the leaves have curled a spray reaches much less.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Usually no treatment: UGA has the psyllid often limited by natural parasites and holds any insecticide until damage has been observed, and NC State describes, on native persimmon, populations that are temporarily abundant and then decline as parasitic wasps and other natural enemies catch up, with egg-to-adult development taking only a few weeks in spring. Conservation is therefore the working control, and pyrethroids, which NC State calls harsh on beneficials, are the wrong tool for it; NC State also advises minimizing the shearing or clipping of terminals during the growing season. Florida's table reads differently, calling for very early control because sprays are less effective once leaves curl, a stance written for an orchard; the home documents govern here. Where a grower does treat a stunted tree, horticultural oil is NC State's choice for sparing beneficials, timed to the first spring flush.

symptoms_seasoned.new: New leaves crinkle, curl and roll around the feeding of the nymphs in spring, and shoot tips can twist and become galled. Inside the distorted leaves are the flattened, white-fluff-covered nymphs, with the small black-bodied adults on the leaf surface; the nymphs also drip honeydew on which sooty mold can grow. Florida lists stunted growth among the symptoms.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Extension gives a persimmon grower one job on this borer: watch for it. Clemson's advice is that it is important to monitor the persimmon borer, and that if borer damage is noted on the trunk or exposed roots, treatment may be required. What to look for, in the signs Florida gives for its tree borers as a group, is gummy sap, droppings or sawdust coming from small holes in the bark, from pruning cuts, or on the trunk near the soil line; Georgia puts this borer's larvae in the lower trunk and tap roots, so the bottom of the trunk and any roots showing above ground are where to look. Raking up under the tree does nothing here, because the larvae are in the wood and the roots, not in anything lying on the ground, and no persimmon guide describes a cleanup step against them. The treatment the guides describe is a preventive insecticide program like the one used for peachtree borer, which Florida times from March through June to stop the larvae getting into the tree, adding that little else is known about controlling it directly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: No home control beyond monitoring and a preventive insecticide program is documented for Sannina uroceriformis. UGA calls it a serious pest of native and oriental persimmons whose larvae attack the lower trunk and tap roots, and says that where infestations occur, preventive insecticide treatments similar to those made for peachtree borer will be required; UF gives the window as March through June applications to keep larvae out of the tree and notes limited direct control information. Clemson's instruction is to monitor, and to treat if damage is noted on the trunk or exposed roots. The signs UF lists for its tree borers as a group, this species among them, are gummy sap, frass or sawdust at small holes, in pruning cuts, or on the trunk near the soil line; for this borer the soil line is the place to read them, since UGA puts its larvae in the lower trunk and tap roots. There is no sanitation target on record for this borer: no persimmon document describes litter, debris or a ground stage for the insect. Wire probing of tunnels is described only for flatheaded borers, a different insect that works the scaffold limbs, and no persimmon document describes it for the persimmon borer.

Georgia calls it a serious pest of both native and oriental persimmons, seen attacking oriental persimmons in Georgia, and Clemson's advice is to monitor for it and to treat if damage is found on the trunk or exposed roots.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This disease is settled by the ground the tree goes into, not by anything sprayed later. UC IPM's persimmon page says the tree tolerates many soils but requires good drainage; its Phytophthora note says to improve drainage before planting, to set a tree on a mound up to 2 feet high with a gradual slope where the soil is heavy, and never to let water stand or the soil stay saturated around the base of the trunk. Let the top few inches of soil dry between waterings, keep soil and mulch off the crown and graft union, and keep any drip emitter well out from the trunk. If a tree is already sick, UC IPM gives one rescue, and only for a tree whose dead patch of bark at the base is small: pull the soil away from the trunk down to the top of the main roots and leave the crown open to the air so it dries out. A tree whose dead patch runs more than about a quarter of the way around the trunk does not usually recover, even with the best care.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The water molds behind this need free water in the soil to move and infect, so drainage is the control and UC IPM says not to rely on fungicides alone. Its persimmon-specific line is the drainage requirement; the generic prescription is drainage improvement before planting, mounds up to 2 feet high for trees, avoidance of prolonged saturation or standing water at the base, drying the top few inches between irrigations, drip emitters set as far from the trunk as the roots allow, and no soil or mulch over the root crown or graft union. Texas A&M frames the same condition from the rootstock side: the native persimmon thrives from sands to bottomland as long as the soils do not stand in water. On a tree already infected, the page's verdict is that a substantial infection rarely recovers and that lesions larger than about one-quarter of the trunk's circumference do not typically recover even with ideal care; smaller lesions can sometimes be saved by removing soil from the base of the tree down to the top of the main roots and allowing the crown tissue to dry out, which is drying rather than cutting, and so sits with drainage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The roots decide how exposed the tree is. Asian persimmon on its own roots is highly susceptible to root rot; the native American persimmon it is normally grafted onto is only moderately susceptible and tolerates wet soil, and Texas A&M says it is critical that every Asian persimmon be grafted onto it because root rot is prevalent wherever the tree can grow. When you buy, ask what the tree is grafted on. If a nursery offers a tree on Diospyros lotus roots, that one does not tolerate poorly drained soil and is the wrong choice for a damp site.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rootstock is the only resistance lever, and it is named by species rather than cultivar. Texas A&M's ranking is Texas persimmon resistant, American persimmon moderately susceptible, Oriental persimmon highly susceptible, with grafting onto American persimmon called critical; UF describes D. virginiana as providing a tolerance of wet soils, and UC Davis as having a fibrous root system tolerant of both drought and excess moisture, at the cost of non-uniform trees and suckering. UC Davis rules out D. lotus for wet ground, since it does not tolerate poorly drained soils. Tolerance is relative: the native rootstock is less susceptible than kaki on its own roots, not immune, so it stacks on drainage rather than replacing it.

control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's leaf-spot guidance is to avoid overhead sprinklers and to irrigate early in the day so the foliage dries more quickly; the target is leaf-wetness duration through the spring infection window. It buys nothing against rain, which is what a wet spring supplies, and it is a delivery and scheduling choice rather than a treatment.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Most persimmons never need a spray for leaf spot: UC IPM says fungicide treatment is generally not warranted for leaf spots, and Texas A&M says only severe cases warrant treatment. A severe case is a tree that dropped its leaves in late August in past years, right as the fruit was ripening, because that is when the disease costs you: fruit that does not sweeten or ripen properly, a crop only every other year, and a tree more easily hurt by freezes. For that tree, chlorothalonil is the protectant Arkansas names as labeled for this leaf spot on persimmon, timed as a cover spray at full bloom and again 3 to 4 weeks later. Chlorothalonil carries a bee precaution against spraying anything in flower, so a bloom-time application has to fit the evening window the label allows, if it allows one. Check that the label lists persimmon, wear gloves, long sleeves and goggles, and keep it out of ponds and drains.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A rescue reserved for the severe case. UAEX's timing is a fungicide cover spray during full bloom and again 3 to 4 weeks later, and it names two labeled products, a chlorothalonil formulation and a strobilurin with no counterpart in the home materials here; UC IPM's general position is that fungicide treatment is not warranted for leaf spots, and Texas A&M's that only severe cases warrant it. The infection window UAEX gives, shoot expansion, leaf formation and flowering, is why the first spray sits at bloom, and that slot collides with chlorothalonil's honey-bee precaution, which confines any application over open flowers to the sunset-to-midnight window a label may allow. The severity threshold UAEX supplies is defoliation in late August as the fruit ripens, with the sugar, ripening, biennial-bearing and freeze consequences that follow.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Small dead spots on the leaves that grow into angular lesions and can merge into larger blotches; affected leaves yellow and fall early. The infection takes place in spring, at shoot expansion, leaf formation and flowering, and shows later in the season. In a severe year the tree can defoliate in late August as the fruit begins to ripen, and that is where the harm lies: fruit sugar fails to accumulate, fruit ripens poorly, the tree tends toward bearing every other year, and it is more vulnerable to freeze damage. It is not deadly to a mature tree, and most years it is minor on a crop extension calls largely free of serious disease.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the canopy open enough that air moves through it. Florida's guide lists maintaining good airflow in the canopy among the practices that reduce this disease, and it also says heavy pruning of persimmon is often not required or beneficial, so the aim is an open, uncrowded tree rather than a hard cutback. Give a young tree room from its neighbors and from walls, and thin crowded growth lightly instead of shearing it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: One of the incidence-reducers in UF's Botryosphaeria cell is maintaining good airflow in the canopy, alongside pruning practice and stress reduction. UF adds that heavy pruning of persimmon is often not required or beneficial, which sets the scale: openness by site and light thinning, since the same document's other lever is keeping stress off the tree. UF states the practice without a mechanism, and no persimmon document supplies one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: There is no good chemical control for this disease, so the pruning saw is the tool, and how you prune matters as much as what you cut. Take out dead and dying twigs and any dead, diseased or broken branch, which the persimmon guides call for as ordinary pruning, and get the prunings away from the tree. Prune only on dry days, and wipe or dip your tools between cuts so you are not carrying the fungus to the next branch. When shaping a young tree, keep the branches at wide angles to the trunk: Florida ties this disease to bark cracking at the limb joints and asks for wide crotch angles, and Texas takes out narrow-crotched limbs because they create dead areas on the limbs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UF's control cell for Botryosphaeria canker begins with no good chemical control and then names the practices: pruning to wide crotch angles, pruning during dry days, disinfecting tools, maintaining airflow, reducing water or nutrient stress, and a fungicide program, all recommended to reduce incidence rather than to cure. The pruning practices are what this carries: dry-day pruning, tool disinfection between cuts and wide crotch angles at training. Removal of dead and diseased wood rests on the general persimmon pruning guidance rather than on the Botryosphaeria cell (UC IPM's prune out suckers or dead wood in established trees; Texas A&M's remove crossover, shaded, diseased and broken branches; Clemson's remove dead or injured branches), and no persimmon document sets a margin for cutting back below a canker, so none is given. The symptom cell describes discoloration of the wood and deep, elongated bark scars, and the second UF row naming B. dothidea adds leafless terminal twigs, shoot decline and bark cracking at limb joints. Clemson notes that chemical control on large trees is usually not feasible for want of coverage. Expect management, not eradication: UF has the fungus limiting Japanese persimmons in the Deep South to about 8 to 12 years.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Discolored wood and deep, elongated scars in the bark of limbs and trunk. In the symptoms Florida attributes to Botryosphaeria together with Phomopsis and Verticillium, twigs at the branch ends die back and stand leafless, leaves and fruit may be small, shoots wilt and decline, and bark cracks at the limb joints. Florida's guide calls this disease the limiting factor for growing persimmons in Florida and the Deep South, and says it often limits the lifetime of a Japanese persimmon to about 8 to 12 years or less. Clemson lists twig dieback among South Carolina's persimmon diseases.
